meta.description: Cicero, De Legibus III.iii.8 — “Ollis salus populi suprema lex esto.” The Latin is certain; this English wording has no identified translator.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Let the welfare of the people be the ultimate law'?
meta.ogDescription: Cicero wrote it, in a draft law code. The Latin is exact; the familiar English is one of several uncredited renderings, and the 19th-century version reads differently.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 106–43 BC · Roman statesman, orator and philosopher
answer.sourceLine: Cicero wrote it, but not in English and not quite as a slogan. The line comes from De Legibus (On the Laws), Book III — a draft legal code Cicero composed for an ideal republic — where the Latin reads “Ollis salus populi suprema lex esto”: for them, the welfare of the people shall be the supreme law. The “them” matters: the clause is addressed to the holders of consular power, who have just been told they answer to no one. This exact English wording, though, is of unknown authorship. Wikiquote ↗ prints it with no translator credited, and the nineteenth-century Bohn translation renders the same clause as “for the safety of the people is the supreme law.”
answer.confidenceText: The attribution is secure and precisely located — Cicero’s Latin sentence is quoted below from De Legibus 3.3.8. What is not established is who produced this particular English rendering: no source consulted names a translator for it, and the 1853 Bohn translation words the same clause differently.

source.excerpt: Regio imperio duo sunto, iique … praetores iudices consules appellamino. Militiae summum ius habento, nemini parento. Ollis salus populi suprema lex esto.
trail: The Latin was read first-hand in De legibus, Liber III ↗: section marker 8 carries “Regio imperio duo sunto … Militiae summum ius habento, nemini parento. Ollis salus populi suprema lex esto.”

Wikipedia’s article on the phrase ↗ gives the same locator — “book III, part III, sub. VIII” — and offers several English versions, including “Let the good [or safety] of the people be the supreme [or highest] law” and “The welfare of the people shall be the supreme law.” None is the wording quoted here.

The nineteenth-century Bohn translation was checked directly. In The Treatises of M.T. Cicero ↗ (London: H. G. Bohn, 1853), the passage reads “Let them have supreme authority over the army, and let them be subject to none; for the safety of the people is the supreme law” — same sense, different words.

Wikiquote’s sourced Cicero page ↗ carries the wording used here and cites “Book III, section 3,” naming no translator. Its neighbouring entries do credit theirs (Barham, Yonge), which is why the omission is worth flagging rather than filling in.
Note on the locator: “Book III, section 3” is the chapter. The section number within it is 8, which is why the usual scholarly citation is 3.3.8.
source.excerptNote: The Latin as it stands in De legibus, Liber III on Latin Wikisource ↗, at section marker 8. The quoted maxim is the last clause; the sentences before it are what ollis (“for them”) refers back to.

source.rightsNote: Cicero’s Latin is unquestionably in the public domain — he died in 43 BC. The English wording shown is a different matter: no source consulted names its translator or the edition it came from, so quotle.info asserts no rights status for it rather than guessing. Readers who need a translation of known provenance can use the 1853 Bohn version linked above, which is public domain.

author.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.heading: About Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.metaLine: 106–43 BC · Roman statesman, lawyer, orator and philosopher
author.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero (3 January 106 BC – 7 December 43 BC) wrote De Legibus as a companion to his De Re Publica: a dialogue that stops arguing about law in the abstract and simply drafts one, in deliberately archaic legal Latin. That is why this line reads like statute rather than philosophy — it is statute, written for a republic that existed only on the page, by a man watching the real one come apart.

misattribution.heading: What to watch for
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is credited with this line. The problems are the wording and the locator.

items.why: Secure. The Latin sits in De legibus, Liber III ↗ at section 8, and Wikipedia ↗ gives the same locator.

items.who: “Let the welfare of the people be the ultimate law”
items.why: Widely repeated, including on Wikiquote ↗, always without a translator. The 1853 Bohn edition reads “for the safety of the people is the supreme law,” and Wikipedia lists three further variants. Treat the English as a gloss, not a quotation from a known edition.

The maxim is almost always quoted without its first word. Ollis is archaic Latin for illis — “for them” — and it ties the rule to the consuls just granted supreme military authority. Dropped, the sentence becomes a general principle; in Cicero’s draft it is a limit on named office-holders.
A common citation, and it names the chapter. The section is 8, so the standard reference is De Legibus 3.3.8 — which is what Wikipedia ↗ gives as “book III, part III, sub. VIII.”

misattribution.truthLine: Cicero wrote the sentence; the English you have seen is anonymous, and the version that circulates has quietly lost the word that said who it applied to.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line has had a long second career. It is the state motto of Missouri and of the University of Missouri, and it appears on the Seal of Missouri; it is also a standing citation in constitutional argument, usually invoked to justify emergency powers — which is close to the opposite of its position in Cicero’s text.

In De Legibus it is a constraint. The consuls have just been told they hold supreme military authority and answer to nobody; the very next clause tells them what they are for. The maxim is the leash, not the licence.
detailsBody: Cicero wrote the law code in deliberately archaic Latin — sunto, habento, parento, esto — the imperative forms of real Roman statute, to make his invented laws sound ancient rather than new. That style is why the sentence quotes so well: it already reads like something carved rather than argued. It is also why the loss of ollis goes unnoticed. A statute addressed to particular magistrates, stripped of its addressee, turns into a maxim addressed to everybody, and a clause limiting power starts doing duty as one that expands it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Latin Wikisource's De legibus, Liber III carries at section marker 8: 'Regio imperio duo sunto, iique a praeeundo iudicando consulendo praetores iudices consules appellamino. Militiae summum ius habento, nemini parento. Ollis salus populi suprema lex esto.'

Wikipedia states the phrase comes from Cicero's De Legibus 'book III, part III, sub. VIII', offers English renderings including 'Let the good [or safety] of the people be the supreme [or highest] law' and 'The welfare of the people shall be the supreme law', and confirms it is the state motto of Missouri and of the University of Missouri and appears on the Seal of Missouri.

The Bohn edition The Treatises of M.T. Cicero (London: H.G. Bohn, 1853) renders the passage 'Let them have supreme authority over the army, and let them be subject to none; for the safety of the people is the supreme law'.

Wikiquote's sourced Cicero page lists 'Salus populi suprema lex esto.' with the English 'Let the welfare of the people be the ultimate law.' under De Legibus, citing 'Book III, section 3', and names no translator, although adjacent entries credit Francis Barham and C. D. Yonge.
Wikipedia gives Cicero's dates as 3 January 106 BC to 7 December 43 BC.
